compliance.notes: Strong core compliance (23 of 24 core requirements score >=2). Standout strengths: an exemplary liability benchmark charted separately for the General Fund and HRA out to ~2095 with all four balances (LB-01/02/04), a fully reconciled CFR (PI-02), an SLY-driven counterparty matrix using CDS beyond ratings (INV-01/03), a full-Council MRP policy with the VRP position disclosed (MRP-02), an integrated two-pool borrowing strategy (BOR-01) and a genuinely strategic capital strategy with proportionality analysis (CS-01). The single core gap is RISK-02 (interest-rate exposure) scored 1 - a qualitative interest-rate strategy and maturity-structure limits exist but no explicit fixed-vs-variable exposure limits are set. Other notable weaknesses: treasury scrutiny is assigned to the Cabinet/executive rather than an independent committee (GOV-04); no treasury ESG policy (ESG-01, 0); no audit-qualification flag (RPT-05, 0) or MRP-in-accounts disclosure (MRP-03, 0) in the scored documents; no explicit monetary cap on loans to external bodies (COM-09); and no MiFID II status disclosure (INV-07). The document sits within a severely stressed budget (Exceptional Financial Support reliance, among the lowest reserves of any UA, S114 risk if EFS refused), which the strategy reflects but does not fully stress-test for affordability.

gaps.evidence: cover report §12.3 p.18 the Capital Strategy and TMSS are 'compliant with the new code and do not include capital investment activity where the primary purpose is commercial yield'; Capital Strategy(App5) §1.4/§5.4

Capital Strategy(App5) §7.6 p.10 'No overall cap has been set on the total loan value that may be provided to external bodies. Each loan is considered on its own merits'; no aggregate service/commercial investment limit stated

TMSS(App6) §4.4.1/§4.4.4 pp.19-20 pooled funds addressed (money market funds and ultra/short-dated bond funds with limits; Royal London bond funds in §4.1.1 p.16); no MiFID II professional-client status disclosure found in either document
TMSS(App6) §4.2(xi) p.18 and §4.4.1 p.19 all investments sterling-denominated; borrowing is PWLB/market/LA (sterling) but no explicit sterling-only borrowing statement

news_drafts.headline: Brighton and Hove faces £20.9m overspend, requests £30m government loan
news_drafts.lead: Brighton and Hove Council is requesting permission from government to borrow an additional £30m — known as exceptional financial support — after forecasting a £20.852m overspend for 2026/27. The council has warned that if the request is denied, its chief finance officer will file a Section 114 notice, a formal warning that the council cannot balance its budget from income. The overspend stems from three main pressures: temporary accommodation (£12m), adult social care placements (£12m), and schools funding for special educational needs (£8.925m). The council's transformation programmes are on track but cannot keep pace with rising demand and costs. A CIPFA review found financial resilience weaknesses; the council reports improvements are being implemented, with a follow-up assessment scheduled for end of September.

news_drafts.headline: Brighton and Hove faces severe budget crisis as adult social care demand outpaces savings
news_drafts.lead: Brighton and Hove is forecasting an overspend of £20.852m on its main operating budget in 2026/27, with additional risks of £16.949m, driven primarily by soaring demand in adult social care and temporary accommodation. The council's transformation programmes are delivering projects on time, but savings are being overwhelmed by rising demand and costs. Residential placements in adult social care cost around £20,000 per week, with small changes in placement numbers significantly affecting the forecast. Temporary accommodation faces a £12m budget increase, but only £5.14m of proposed mitigations. The council is requesting government borrowing of up to £30m, called Exceptional Financial Support, to cover the shortfall. It warns that without approval, the chief financial officer must file a Section 114 notice, a formal warning that the council cannot balance its budget.

findings.headline: £300k savings from Brickfields accommodation project dependent on successful outsourced service delivery and timely mobilization
findings.detail: The council proposes £300k in savings by relocating service users from expensive out-of-city accommodation to a new 28-apartment Brickfields facility. The paper notes this assumes service provision will be outsourced and mobilization will not be significantly delayed. The council identifies this as a positive development that should bring service users closer to families, but delivery depends on external parties and timely execution.
findings.matters: Service transformation depending on outsourcing and timely mobilization; delays or outsourcing failures would reduce or eliminate the £300k saving.
findings.quote: Assumes service provision for new service will be outsourced and mobilisation of service is not significantly delayed.

findings.headline: £400k Adult Social Care savings from closing Wellington House day service dependent on sufficient capacity in independent sector providers
findings.detail: The council proposes to close the in-house Wellington House day service and reprrovision services through the independent and non-profit sector following a statutory Care Act review, targeting £400k in savings. The paper identifies as a delivery risk: capacity in day options market to meet need. If the private and non-profit market cannot absorb demand, savings may not be realized and service users could face gaps in provision.
findings.matters: This is statutory service reprovision where market-dependent delivery could fail, resulting in both unachieved savings and service delivery failures affecting the council's financial outturn.
findings.quote: Capacity in day options market to meet need.

findings.headline: £12m forecast pressure on Temporary Accommodation partially addressed by £5.14m in proposed savings with material delivery risks
findings.detail: The paper identifies a severe financial pressure on Temporary Accommodation with a forecast increase of £12m on the net General Fund. The council proposes £5.14m in savings through four workstreams (increasing supply, cost recovery, homelessness prevention, and accelerating move-on), leaving an identified funding gap of at least £6.86m. The paper explicitly flags that delivery risks including increasing demand, affordability constraints in the housing market, and limited capacity in partner and support services could impact the pace and sustainability of savings delivery and require close monitoring.
findings.matters: Temporary Accommodation is a statutory service and this reveals an unfunded pressure with uncertain mitigation; lenders need to know about material budget pressures affecting statutory services.
findings.figures: forecast increase of £12m on the net General Fund; £5.14m in proposed savings
findings.quote: The budget for Temporary Accommodation is under severe financial pressure, with a forecast increase of £12m on the net General Fund. Four key workstreams are established, which will reduce the pressure, totalling £5.14m

findings.headline: CIPFA review on behalf of MHCLG identified financial resilience and control weaknesses; follow-up assessment scheduled for end of September.
findings.detail: The council underwent external CIPFA review of financial resilience and organizational response to budget pressures on behalf of MHCLG. Recommendations were issued and the council reports these are being or have been implemented. The council notes all highlighted areas were already known internally. A follow-up visit is scheduled for end of September.
findings.matters: External regulator identified financial management weaknesses warranting formal review; follow-up visit signals ongoing concern about remediation progress.
findings.quote: BHCC has undergone a review by CIPFA on behalf of MHCLG which scrutinised our financial resilience and our organisational response to the budgetary pressures that we're facing.

findings.headline: £8.925m Dedicated Schools Grant overspend from High Needs Block demand, with Department for Education scrutiny in preparation for potential partial write-off.
findings.detail: The DSG overspend reflects increased demand in the High Needs Block. The Department for Education is currently scrutinizing councils' accumulated DSG overspends in preparation for potential partial write-off. While BHCC is noted as compliant with lower overspends than most other councils, the council acknowledges "a potential threat" due to the overall value of DSG expenditure.
findings.matters: DfE scrutiny creates uncertainty about future DSG recovery; the council-managed ring-fenced account carries unresolved liability if write-off does not occur.
findings.quote: The Department for Education continues to scrutinise closely the past expenditure on the DSG, as it is doing with all Councils currently in preparation for the partial write off of overspends.
